newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian Innogenetics sees bright future on Easdaq.
newsitem.headline: Belgian Innogenetics sees bright future on Easdaq.

text.p: Belgian biotechnology firm Innogenetics, set to become one of the first companies listed on Europe's new growth stocks market Easdaq, said on Tuesday its strong patent portfolio would help it secure a bright future.
"We are on the verge of exceptional growth," chief executive Hugo Van Heuverswyn told a news conference.

Brussels-based Easdaq expects 10 to 15 companies to be listed by the end of 1996 and 500 in five years. It was launched at the end of last month, but trade is expected to get underway only now that an administrative hurdle has been cleared.
Van Heuverswyn declined to give information about the listing on Easdaq, short for European Association of Securities Dealers Automated Quotation.
Innogenetics, 12.5 percent owned by Kredietbank, was founded in 1985 but came out of the red only this year.
Van Heuverswyn forecast net profit of 1.316 billion francs in 2000 against a loss of four million in 1995. Total revenue should jump to 5.40 billion francs from 669 million in 1995.
"We have a strong portfolio of 60 patents," he said, adding product development and clinical trials would be accelerated.

Innogenetics has forged a leading position in DNA probe technology. It applies biotechnology for research into the treatment of infection, transplantation, auto-immunity, wound healing, Alzheimer disease and genetic disorders.
Its core products include a fast test for hepatitis C, which can cause liver cirrhosis and liver cancer if left untreated.
Some 300 million people are believed to be infected.
"Problems only show after 10, 15 years. Doctors now can see quickly whether someone is infected," Van Heuverswyn said.
Innogenetics also expects to maintain a unique position in the field of detecting Alzheimer's disease.
It has developed a test to determine whether the tuberculosis bacteria is becoming resistent to certain antibiotics during treatment.
"It will prevent the useless treatment with antibiotics," Van Heuverswyn said.
Innogenetics, which has discovered the subtype O for the HIV virus that causes AIDS, has also developed its own quick 15-minute AIDS test which requires no special equipment.
"There's especially strong demand from nurses in ambulances," said Van Heuverswyn. The product will not be sold over the counter, though.
Van Heuverswyn added Innogenetics had a sheer monopoly in some areas such as detecting Alzheimer.

Ghent-based Innogenetics is expected to wipe out competition with a new product, due to be launched next year, which detects the presence of AIDS virus variants that became resistant to AZT or other drugs during treatment.
"This will be one of our biggest products," said Van Heuverswyn, who expected the product to account for 300 to 400 million dollars in turnover within three to four years.
"Nobody has this product, and even if they had it, they would not be allowed to sell it," he said.
Another key product is a rapid test for rejection of organ or skin tissue after transplants.
Van Heuverswyn said Innogenetics planned to construct a new manufacturing unit in Flanders, which would cost between 400 and 600 million francs and create more than 300 jobs.
It plans to set up a manufacturing plant in the U.S. by the end of 1997 to produce and sell products with FDA approval.
Van Heuverswyn said Innogenetics might also set up subsidiaries, for instance in the field wound healing.
"We're looking at other companies which are working in the same area," Van Heuverswyn said.
Innogenetics chairman Rudi Marien said its tests would lead to considerable savings in the health care sector.
"There's a major potential. By the year 2010, 50 percent of all drugs will be biotechnological products," Marien said.
Innogenetics now has over 40 diagnostic products on the market and will launch another 28 in the next three years.
It predicted its R&D cost/product sales ratio, current at 80 percent, would fall to between 20 and 25 percent.
